title: Iwo To Field Carrier Landing Practice
description: Pilots assigned to Carrier Air Wing (CVW) 5 participate in field carrier landing practice at Iwo To, Japan. Formerly known as Iwo Jima, Iwo To is an island roughly 750 miles south of Tokyo used by CVW 5 to conduct yearly fighter pilot training and qualifications.
keywords: jets, NPASE, Carrier Air Wing 5, Iwo To, Mt. Suribachi, Aviation News, training, navy, Marine Corps, Japan, F/A-18, CVW 5, pilot, super hornet, Iwo Jima
credit: Petty Officer 3rd Class Raymond Diaz III

transcript.text: - [Pilot] This is Mount Suribachi off
our left side and Invasion Beach.
^- [PO Diaz] This small Pacific island
^accessed only by military aircraft
may look picturesque but this is no vacation spot.
Iwo To, formerly known as IwoJima and located
750 miles south of the Japanese mainland
is where in 1945 American and Japanese forces
battled for control over the island
and its vital air fields.
(jet noise)
^- [CDR Pitta] Iwo To is our temporary facility
^while we await the identification
^of a permanent facility here in Japan
for our field/carrier landing practice.
(jet noise)
We've been using it for many years.
It gives us an authentic replication
of the environment out at the ship.
Again, it gives us very good training
for our operations in the carrier qualification
and then shipboard operations.
- [PO Diaz] More than 70 years later
Iwo To and it's modern day airfield
provide pilots from Carrier Airwing 5 an
opportunity to practice and perfect
launching, landing and touch-and-go qualifications.
- [CDR Pitta] The majority of aircraft
you'll see out there with American markings
on them will be the Superhornets from Carrier Airwing 5.
That includes the Echo, Fox, and Gulf models
so the fighters and the jammers.
They'll be out there again for about 10 days
as the squadrons rotate through their training.
- [PO Diaz] Aside form practicing during the day,
pilots also train at night as part
of their training routine.
(jet noise)
Pilots practice a total of three daytime practices
and three nighttime practices.
This is half the time pilots in the US
pilots get to train and qualify due to the
high operational tempo of the forward deployed carrier.
The squadrons will rotate through
training within a 10 day period.
- [CDR Pitta] So we maintain both our combat
effectiveness for our alliance requirements
here in Japan and the peer requirements.
And also to do it safely so we can protect
our families and the Japanese people.
- [PO Diaz] Field/carrier landing practice is one
of the many ways our forward deployed
naval force stays mission ready.
Reporting from Iwo To, Japan,
I'm Petty Officer Raymond Diaz.
